section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The antipodal points
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere and antipodal points (two points exactly opposite on a sphere). State the core premise: If we look at temperature or pressure on Earth, there must exist two opposite points with identical conditions.
section_1.example: Visualize a 3D Earth globe; as you rotate it, identify two points 'North Pole' and 'South Pole' mapping to a shared weather condition value.

section_2.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem (Mathematical Foundation)
section_2.content: Formalize the theorem: Any continuous function from an n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space maps at least one pair of antipodal points to the same value. Use a visual 'height mapping' animation on a topographical map.
section_2.example: A hiker walking around a mountain range; the theorem guarantees there are always two opposite spots on the mountain with the exact same altitude.

section_3.title: Transition: From Spheres to Necklaces
section_3.content: Bridge the gap: Explain how we represent discrete items (like beads on a necklace) as a continuous interval (0 to 1). This connects topology to combinatorial problems.
section_3.example: An animation showing beads of two colors (gold and silver) being 'stretched' along a line segment to represent their density distribution.

section_4.title: The Stolen Necklace Problem
section_4.content: Define the problem: Two thieves steal a necklace with n types of beads. They want to cut it into pieces such that each thief gets exactly half of each type of bead. State the theorem: For k thieves and n types of beads, at most k(n-1) cuts are needed.
section_4.example: Two burglars (Alice and Bob) with a necklace containing 10 rubies and 10 diamonds. The animation shows them making precise cuts to split the loot perfectly using the Borsuk-Ulam result.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-world Insight
section_5.content: Conclude by emphasizing the beauty of 'Topological Combinatorics': how high-level geometry provides efficient algorithmic solutions for fair division problems.
section_5.example: Final slide showing a complex cake-cutting machine or a resource allocation dashboard using these principles to ensure fairness in distribution.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.0 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary and Real-world Insight", [
            "Geometry provides elegant solutions.", 
            "Fair division ensures equity.", 
            "Algorithms apply these principles."
        ])
        
        # Visuals
        text_fairness = Text("Fairness", font_size=36, color=GOLD)
        text_symmetry = Text("Symmetry", font_size=36, color=GOLD)
        
        self.place_at_grid(text_fairness, "B2")
        self.place_at_grid(text_symmetry, "E5")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN),
                  FadeIn(text_fairness))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(ORANGE),
                  FadeIn(text_symmetry))
        self.wait(2)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(VGroup(*self.mobjects)))
